title: Deuxième partie : variations sur l'équation des lacets [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois…, pages 293 à 650, dont table des matières] : notes et copies de notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from pages 523 and 525). Grothendieck works with his 'equation des lacets' group, written Γ_Q^~ = Γ_{0,3}^~. This is a combinatorial substitute for Gal(Q̄/Q), a GT-type group. Its elements are pairs (α,β) of elements of the profinite fundamental group Π̂_{0,3} satisfying α ρ(α)^{-1} = β σ(β)^{-1} ℓ_1^ν.

The groups involved are:
- 𝔖^{+∧}_{0,3} ≅ PSL(2,Z)^ = (Z/3 * Z/2)^, the profinite oriented cartographic group of trivalent maps. Here ρ has order 3 and σ has order 2.
- M_{0,3}^~, a 'Teichmüller–Galois' group: an extension of Γ_Q^~ by PSL(2,Z)^.
- A canonical homomorphism (2) from M_{0,3}^~ to GL(2,Ẑ)/±1, coming from the action on the abelianised/Tate-module level.

Step 1 (page 523). Define N_{1,1}^~ as the pullback, along (2), of the central extension 1→{±1}→GL(2,Ẑ)→GL(2,Ẑ)/±1→1. So N_{1,1}^~ is a ±1-extension of M_{0,3}^~.

Step 2 (this page, (4)–(5)). Restrict to the preimage of PSL(2,Z)^ ⊂ M_{0,3}^~. Its pullback is PSL(2,Z)^ ×_{PSL(2,Ẑ)} SL(2,Ẑ), which is canonically SL(2,Z)^. This works because SL(2,Z)^ → PSL(2,Z)^ is also a central ±1-extension and -1 survives in SL(2,Ẑ); page 525 states this as the cartesian square (10). Hence the exact sequence
(5) 1 → SL(2,Z)^ = T_{1,1}^{+∧} → N_{1,1}^~ → Γ_Q^~ → 1.
T_{1,1}^{+} = SL(2,Z) is the orientation-preserving mapping class group of the once-punctured torus; the NB on page 523 recalls that T_{1,1} ≅ GL(2,Z). So N_{1,1}^~ is the GT-analogue of the arithmetic fundamental group π_1(M_{1,1,Q}).

Step 3 ((6)). This maps onto the 'Tate module of the universal elliptic curve' sequence 1→SL(2,Ẑ)→GL(2,Ẑ)→Ẑ*→1.
- The left vertical map is the congruence-completion surjection SL(2,Z)^ → SL(2,Ẑ).
- The right vertical map is the cyclotomic character χ.

Step 4 ((7)–(9)). Using a base point labelled '0' (tangential-base-point type), M_{0,3}^~ splits as a semi-direct product M_{0,3}^~(0) ⋉ PSL(2,Z)^, with M_{0,3}^~(0) ≅ Γ_Q^~. A canonical lift (8) M_{0,3}^~(0) → GL(2,Ẑ) of the restriction of (2) then gives the splitting (9) N_{1,1}^~ ≅ N_{1,1}^~(0)·SL(2,Z)^. This yields a genuine (not merely outer) action of Γ_Q^~ on SL(2,Z)^.

On page 525 he starts to make this explicit: u(ρ) = int(α)ρ and u(σ) = int(β)σ. This is compatible with conjugation in SL(2,Ẑ).

Purpose: extend the genus-0 'loop equation' group to genus 1, i.e. let the GT-type group act on the profinite Teichmüller group Γ_{1,1}^, mirroring the Galois action on π_1 of the moduli stack of elliptic curves.
errors: Notational slips only. On page 523, Sl(2,Ẑ) is written where SL(2,Z)^ (profinite completion) is meant, in the top row of (1) and in (10).
The '~' and '^' decorations are used inconsistently (N_{1,1} vs N_{1,1}^~; GL(2,Ẑ)^# vs GL(2,Ẑ)).

Mathematically the construction is sound. The pullback restricted to PSL(2,Z)^ is SL(2,Z)^ because both are central ±1-extensions and -1 ≠ 1 in SL(2,Ẑ). Surjectivity of the vertical maps in (6) follows from surjectivity of the congruence map and of χ.
Surjectivity of χ on Γ_Q^~ is used implicitly. It holds since Gal(Q̄/Q) maps into it compatibly.

ideas.what: Defining a GT-analogue of π_1(M_{1,1}/Q) by pulling back the central ±1-extension GL(2,Ẑ) → GL(2,Ẑ)/±1 along the genus-0 group M_{0,3}^~ → GL(2,Ẑ)/±1. This gives 1→SL(2,Z)^→N_{1,1}^~→Γ_Q^~→1.
ideas.modern_name: Action of GT (or a variant) on the profinite mapping class group Γ_{1,1}^ = SL(2,Z)^ (genus-one level of the GT tower)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lochak–Nakamura–Schneps (1997, 'On a new version of the Grothendieck–Teichmüller group'); Nakamura; Ihara for the Galois version
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme mentions the Galois action on SL(2,Z)^ and the Teichmüller tower; this explicit ±1 pullback construction is not, to my knowledge, published

ideas.what: Comparison diagram (6) with the Tate-module sequence 1→SL(2,Ẑ)→GL(2,Ẑ)→Ẑ*→1, with χ as the cyclotomic character.
ideas.modern_name: Monodromy of the universal elliptic curve / congruence quotient of π_1(M_{1,1})
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Shimura, Deligne–Rapoport; Ihara for profinite settings)

ideas.what: Splitting M_{0,3}^~ ≅ Γ_Q^~ ⋉ PSL(2,Z)^ via a base point '0', lifted to a splitting of N_{1,1}^~, giving an honest action of Γ_Q^~ on SL(2,Z)^.
ideas.modern_name: Tangential base point section; GT action on B_3^/center

ideas.what: Identifications T_{1,1} ≅ GL(2,Z) and T_{1,1}^+ ≅ SL(2,Z); PSL(2,Z) as the oriented cartographic group of trivalent maps.
ideas.modern_name: Mapping class group of the once-punctured torus; cartographic group
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical; cartographic group: Grothendieck (Esquisse), Malle–Shabat etc.

missed.claim: Grothendieck explicitly constructs the genus-one extension of his loop-equation (GT-type) group, with its splitting via a base point. The construction is a fibre product with the ±1 central extension of GL(2,Ẑ). He thereby obtains an action of Γ_Q^~ on SL(2,Z)^ lifting the cyclotomic character. This anticipates the genus-one part of Lochak–Nakamura–Schneps's later work.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is historical priority for the GT action on Γ_{1,1}. It is also a slick construction (pullback of the elliptic-involution extension) that avoids braid-group computations.

missed.claim: He sets out to make the action of Γ_Q^~ on SL(2,Z)^ explicit in terms of (α,β) and the twisted loop equation with the ℓ_1^ν term (page 525). The explicit formulas and their compatibility are not completed on these pages.
missed.quote: Ainsi on a une opération de Γ_Q^~ sur Sl(2,Z)^ que je voudrais expliciter
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: The ν-twisted loop equation variant may correspond to a slightly larger GT-type group than Drinfeld's. Comparing it with GT-hat and with the LNS GT' could be of minor interest.

deep.surprise_reason: This is an unpublished but natural genus-one extension of Grothendieck's GT-type group, made via an elegant pullback. The content (GT acting on SL(2,Z)^) is known in the later literature (Lochak–Nakamura–Schneps, Nakamura), so it is mainly of historical and priority interest.
